question: What three verbs of posture (walking, standing, sitting) appear in verse 1, and what progression do they suggest?
What contrast does the psalm draw between the tree planted by the streams of water and the chaff the wind drives away?
The verb הָגָה (hagah, “murmur, meditate”) also describes a low sound: what kind of meditation on the Law does it suggest?
The righteous man “delights” in the Law of the LORD: what feeds your day and your night today?
What do the nations and the kings plot, and against whom do they gather?
Why is the first reaction of the One “enthroned in heaven” to laugh, and what does this laughter say about human plans?
The word מָשִׁיחַ (mashiach, “anointed one”) is applied to the king: how has this title been read in the Jewish and Christian traditions from this psalm?
The psalm ends with an invitation to the kings and a beatitude: what power or influence do you have that would need to be exercised “with fear”?
According to the title, David was fleeing from Absalom: what do his enemies say about him, and how many times does the word “many” appear?
What images does David use for God in verse 3, and why does “the One who lifts my head” suit a humiliated king in flight?
The verb שָׁכַב (shakhav, “lie down”) in verse 5: what does it mean to be able to lie down and sleep in the middle of a revolt?
What worry has been keeping you from sleep, and how does the experience of verse 5 speak to it?
What advice does the psalmist give to the “sons of men” in verses 2 to 5?
Many ask “who can show us anything good?”: why is the joy of verse 7 compared to an abundance of grain and new wine?
The verb רָחַב (rachav, “make room, enlarge”) appears in verse 1 as “relieved”: what image of space does it set against distress, which is a narrow place?
“Be angry, yet do not sin”: what do you usually do with your anger before going to sleep?
At what time of day does the psalmist lay out his prayer, and what does he do after praying?
How does the psalmist distinguish himself from his enemies, and on what does he base his entry into God's house?
The verb צָפָה (tsafah, “watch, wait”) is the verb of the watchman on the tower: what attitude toward God's answer does it describe?
What would it be like to begin the day laying your “cry” before God and staying alert for the answer?
What physical signs of suffering does the psalmist describe in verses 6 and 7?
What changes abruptly from verse 8 on, and how can this turn be explained when the outward situation has not changed yet?
The verb בָּהַל (bahal, “be dismayed, terrified”) appears for the bones, the soul and, at the end, the enemies: what does this repetition do in the psalm?
The psalmist asks “how long?”: what long wait could you bring to God with this same frankness?
What oath does the psalmist make in verses 3 to 5, and what does he accept to suffer if he is guilty?
What images show evil turning back on the one who does it, and what view of justice do they reveal?
The verb שׁוּב (shuv, “turn, return”) appears in verse 12 and verse 16: how does it link repentance to the return of evil upon the unjust?
Asking God to judge “according to my righteousness” requires an honest conscience: how do you examine yours when facing an accusation?
With what sentence does the psalm begin and end, and what lies between these two frames?
What relationship is there between looking at the heavens, “the work of Your fingers,” and the question “what is man”?
The verb פָּקַד (paqad, “visit, care for”) in verse 4: what kind of attention from God does it describe?
Human beings are given rule over animals, birds and fish: how do you understand this responsibility for creation today?
How many acts of praise does the psalmist promise in verses 1 and 2?
The nations fall into the pit and the net they themselves made: how is this pattern described as God's judgment?
The word מִשְׂגָּב (misgav, “refuge, high place”) appears twice in verse 9: what image of protection does it bring to the afflicted?
“The needy will not always be forgotten”: who near you needs to hear this, and how can you make it visible?
What does the wicked man say “in his heart” in verses 6 and 11, and how does this show in his actions?
The psalm begins by asking why the LORD stands far off: how does the end of the psalm answer, or not answer, this question?
The verb שָׁכַח (shakhach, “forget”) appears in the mouth of the wicked (v. 11) and in the psalmist's prayer (v. 12): what contrast does this create?
God is called the “helper of the fatherless”: what vulnerable person near you needs someone who sees them?
What advice is given to the psalmist in verse 1, and what arguments support this advice in verses 2 and 3?
Why does the answer to the question about the destroyed foundations begin by looking at the temple and the throne in heaven?
The verb בָּחַן (bachan, “test, examine”) appears in verses 4 and 5: what does it mean to say the LORD tests the righteous and not only the wicked?
“Flee like a bird to your mountain”: in what situation have you felt like fleeing, and what does the psalm propose instead?
What sins of speech does the psalm list in verses 2 to 4?
Why are the words of the LORD described as silver refined seven times right after so many false words?
The word חֶלְקָה (chelqah, “smoothness”) describes the lips that flatter falsely: what image does it suggest about flattery?
“Our lips are our own”: in what situations do you treat your words as if you did not have to give an account of them?
How many times does the question “how long” appear, and what does it refer to in each case?
The psalm moves from complaint to song without saying that anything outside has changed: what can explain this turn?
The verb בָּטַח (batach, “trust”) in verse 5 comes right after four unanswered questions: what kind of trust does it describe here?
What “how long” question have you been keeping to yourself, and what would change if you said it in prayer like the psalmist?
What does the fool say in his heart, and how does the LORD assess humanity in verses 2 and 3?
What relationship does the psalm draw between denying God and devouring the people as one eats bread?
The word נָבָל (naval, “fool”) points more to a moral failure than an intellectual one: how does this change the reading of “there is no God”?
At what moments do you live as if God were not watching, even without denying Him in words?
What attitudes does the psalm require of someone who wants to dwell in the LORD's tent, and how many of them have to do with how we treat our neighbor?
The question of verse 1 speaks of a “tent” and a “holy mountain”: what place and what kind of life with God do these images evoke?
The verb גּוּר (gur, “sojourn, dwell as a guest”) refers to someone who lives in a land not their own: what does this suggest about the condition of those who dwell in God's tent?
Keeping one's word “even when it hurts”: is there a commitment you are tempted to break because it became costly?
What images of inheritance and land does the psalmist use in verses 5 and 6 to speak of the LORD?
How can verse 10 be read in the psalmist's life, and why was it so important in Christian preaching about the resurrection?
The word נָעִים (na’im, “pleasant”) appears in verse 6 and verse 11: what link does it make between the inheritance received and God's presence?
“I have set the LORD always before me”: what concrete practice would help you do this in your day?
What images describe the protection asked for and the danger of the enemies in verses 8 to 12?
What contrast is there between the “men of this world” and the psalmist's satisfaction in verse 15?
The word כָּנָף (kanaf, “wing”) appears in the image of the shadow of the wings: where else does this image arise in the Bible, and what does it convey?
The psalmist accepts being examined “at night”: what would your heart reveal if it were tested today?
How many titles does the psalmist give the LORD in verse 2, and what do they have in common?
Why is David's deliverance narrated with earthquake, fire, darkness and thunder, like a great manifestation of God?
The adjective תָּמִים (tamim, “blameless, perfect”) appears for the man (v. 23, 25) and for God's way (v. 30, 32): what link does the psalm make between the two?
“You light my lamp”: in what dark area of your life do you need this light in order to scale the wall?
What six names does God's word receive in verses 7 to 9, and what does each one do for those who receive it?
How does the psalm link the silent voice of the heavens to the spoken law, and why does it move from the sun to the Law?
The verb סָתַר (satar, “hide”) appears in the sun from which “nothing is hidden” and in the “hidden” faults: what relationship does the psalm suggest between the two?
What words and thoughts of yours would you like to be “pleasing” before God this week?
Who speaks in verses 1 to 5, and what does this group wish for the king before the battle?
What contrast does verse 7 draw between chariots, horses and the name of the LORD, at a time when these were the strongest weapons?
The word שֵׁם (shem, “name”) appears in verses 1, 5 and 7: what does it mean to trust in God's name and not only in God in a vague way?
What are the “chariots” and “horses” you usually trust in when things get tight?
What gifts has the LORD granted the king, according to verses 2 to 6?
Verse 7 stands at the center of the psalm: how does the king's trust link the first part (what God has given) to the second (what God will do with the enemies)?
The עֲטָרָה (atarah, “crown”) of pure gold is set on the king's head: what does the psalm suggest about who gives the crown and whose is the king's strength?
The king received “his heart's desire”: what desire of yours have you been bringing to God, and how ready are you to hear a yes or a no?
What animals and what actions of the enemies appear in verses 12 to 18 to describe the psalmist's suffering?
The Gospels put verse 1 in the mouth of Jesus on the cross: how does the rest of the psalm, which ends in praise, help us hear this cry?
The word קָהָל (qahal, “congregation, assembly”) appears in verses 22 and 25: why must the praise of the one who was delivered be spoken before the assembly?
The psalmist remembers that God cared for him “from the womb”: what memories of your story help you pray when God seems distant?
At what point does the psalm stop speaking of the LORD in the third person (“He”) and begin speaking to Him (“You”)?
How does the image change in verse 5, from shepherd to host, and what does it mean to have a table prepared “in the presence of my enemies”?
The verb רָדַף (radaf, “pursue”) usually describes enemies on the hunt: what effect does it have to say that goodness and loving devotion are what “will follow me”?
What “valley of the shadow of death” are you or someone close to you walking through now, and what does the phrase “You are with me” mean there?
What questions does the psalm ask in verse 3, and what four characteristics does it give as an answer in verse 4?
What scene seems to lie behind the gates that lift up their heads and the King of Glory who comes in?
The verb נָשָׂא (nasa, “lift up”) appears in verse 4 (the soul), verse 5 (the blessing) and verses 7 and 9 (the gates): how does this verb unite the parts of the psalm?
If the earth and “all who dwell in it” belong to the LORD, how does this affect the way you use what you call your own?
What verbs of teaching and guiding does the psalmist address to God in verses 4 and 5?
What does the psalmist ask God to remember, and what does he ask Him to forget?
The verb קָוָה (qavah, “wait, hope”) appears in verses 3, 5 and 21: what kind of waiting does this psalm, built in alphabetical order in Hebrew, teach?
The psalmist says he is “lonely and afflicted”: when you feel this way, do you usually tell God so with such frankness?
With whom does the psalmist say he does not sit, and what does he say he does instead?
How does the request “test me, O LORD” fit with the claim that he walks in integrity, without turning into pride?
The verb רָחַץ (rachats, “wash”) appears in the gesture of washing the hands in innocence: what link does it have with the rites of purification before approaching the altar?
The psalmist loves “the place where Your glory dwells”: where have you experienced God's presence?
What questions and what images of threat appear in verses 1 to 3?
What relationship is there between the one request of verse 4 and the invitation “seek My face” of verse 8?
The verb בָּקַשׁ (baqash, “seek”) appears in verse 4 and verse 8: what does the psalmist seek, and why is this seeking continual?
The psalm ends with the command to wait, twice: in what situation do you need to hear “wait for the LORD; be strong”?
What does the psalmist fear will happen if God remains silent, and what gesture accompanies his plea?
The psalmist asks that the wicked be repaid according to their deeds: what reason does he give for this in verse 5?
The verb חָרַשׁ (charash, “be deaf, be silent”) in verse 1: why is God's silence felt as a threat of death?
The wicked “speak peace” but have evil in their hearts: how do you deal with the distance between your words and your intentions?
How many times is “the voice of the LORD” repeated, and on what elements of nature does it act?
After so much power and storm, why does the psalm end with strength and peace for the people?
The word קוֹל (qol, “voice, thunder”) can mean both: how does this double meaning help us understand the storm described in the psalm?
In the temple “all cry, ‘Glory!’” while the storm passes: what in you speaks of God when life is turbulent?
From what was the psalmist delivered, according to verses 2 and 3?
What did the psalmist say when he was doing well, and what does this memory reveal about his security?
The word רֶגַע (rega’, “moment”) contrasts with “lifetime” in verse 5: what proportion does the psalm draw between God's anger and His favor?
“You turned my mourning into dancing”: what change like this have you lived through and not yet given thanks for?
What bodily sufferings and what social rejections does the psalmist describe in verses 9 to 13?
Verse 5 appears in the mouth of Jesus in the Gospel of Luke and in Jewish night prayers: what kind of surrender does the phrase “into Your hands I commit my spirit” express?
The word עֵת (et, “time”) is plural in “my times are in Your hands”: what difference does it make to think of life in “times” and not only in years?
The psalmist admits he once said “I am cut off from Your sight”: what hasty conclusion have you drawn in affliction?
What happened to the psalmist while he kept silent, and what changed when he confessed?
Who speaks in verse 8, and why does the image of the horse and mule without understanding come right after?
The verb כָּסָה (kasah, “cover”) appears in the sin “covered” by God (v. 1) and in the sin the psalmist did not hide (v. 5): what interplay is there between these two coverings?
Is there something you have kept in silence that weighs on you as the psalmist describes in verse 3?
How does the psalm describe creation in verses 6 to 9, and what place does God's word have in it?
Why does the psalm say that no army, no strength and no horse guarantee salvation, and what does it put in their place?
The word עֵצָה (etsah, “counsel, plan”) appears in verses 10 and 11: what contrast does the psalm draw between the counsel of the nations and that of the LORD?
The psalm asks for “a new song”: what would make your praise new, and not merely repeated?
What did the psalmist do and what did the LORD do, according to verses 4 to 7?
The title links the psalm to the episode in which David feigned madness before a Philistine king: how does this color the praise “at all times” of verse 1?
The verb טָעַם (ta’am, “taste”) in the invitation “taste and see”: what kind of knowledge of God does this image of the palate suggest?
Of the counsels in verses 13 and 14 (keep your tongue, turn from evil, seek peace), which is the hardest for you right now?
How did the psalmist treat those who now attack him, according to verses 13 and 14, and how did they respond?
The psalmist asks for shame, darkness and ruin for his enemies: how should we read these harsh words in light of the injustice “without cause” he says he suffers?
The verb טָמַן (taman, “hide”) describes the net hidden by the enemies in verses 7 and 8: what justice does the psalmist ask for by using the same image twice?
The psalmist prayed and fasted for people who later betrayed him: what do you do with the pain of having done good and received evil?
What portrait of the wicked does the psalm paint in verses 1 to 4, from thought to action?
What images of height, depth, food and water does the psalmist use for God's goodness right after describing the wicked?
The word מָקוֹר (maqor, “fountain”) in “with You is the fountain of life”: what difference is there between receiving water from a spring and from a cistern?
The wicked man “plots wickedness on his bed”: what usually fills your thoughts before you sleep?
How many times does the advice not to fret appear, and what does the psalm propose in place of fretting?
How should we understand the statement “I have not seen the righteous forsaken” when there are righteous people who do suffer, like Job?
The verb יָרַשׁ (yarash, “inherit, possess”) is repeated in connection with the land: who inherits the land in this psalm, and how does Jesus take up this idea in the Beatitudes?
Whom do you see prospering through dishonesty, and how does the advice “be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him” speak to this envy?
What parts of the body does the psalmist mention when describing his suffering in verses 2 to 10?
What relationship does the psalmist see between his illness and his sin, and how does this reading interact with other texts that question that link?
The word מַשָּׂא (massa, “burden”) in verse 4 compares iniquities to a weight on the back: what does this image say about guilt?
His friends stand “at a distance” from the psalmist's calamity: is there someone suffering from whom you have kept away?
What did the psalmist decide to do in verse 1, and what happened while he kept silent?
Why does the psalmist ask to know the measure of his days, and what portrait of human life does he draw next?
The word הֶבֶל (hevel, “breath, vapor”) appears in verses 5, 6 and 11, and also dominates Ecclesiastes: what view of human life does it convey here?
The psalmist calls himself a “foreigner” and a “stranger” before God: how would this awareness change your plans and your possessions?
What steps of deliverance does the psalmist describe in verses 1 to 3, from the pit to the song?
Why does the psalmist say God did not ask for sacrifices, what does he put in their place, and how does the Letter to the Hebrews reread this passage?
The verb קָוָה (qavah, “wait”) is repeated in verse 1 (“I waited patiently”): what does this emphasis suggest about the time of waiting?
The psalmist does not keep to himself what God has done: with whom could you share something God has been doing in your life?
What do the enemies, and even the close friend, say and do while the psalmist is ill?
Verse 13 is a doxology that closes the first of the five books of the Psalms: why end this collection with a blessing and “Amen and Amen”?
The word דַּל (dal, “weak, poor”) appears in verse 1: why does the psalm begin with the one who cares for the weak, if afterward the weak one is the psalmist himself?
The psalmist was betrayed by one “who shared my bread”: how do you bring to God a wound caused by someone very close?
What images of thirst, food and memory does the psalmist use in verses 1 to 4?
The refrain of verses 5 and 11 (repeated in 43:5) is a conversation of the psalmist with himself: what does this self-exhortation reveal about faith in times of despair?
The word תְּהוֹם (tehom, “deep”) is the same as the watery chaos of Genesis 1: what force does the phrase “deep calls to deep” gain?
Has someone ever asked you, in some way, “where is your God?”, and how does this question echo inside you in hard times?
What does the psalmist ask God to send, and where does he hope to be led?
Verse 5 repeats the refrain of Psalm 42: what clues suggest that the two psalms formed a single poem?
The word שִׂמְחָה (simchah, “joy”) in verse 4 calls God “my exceeding joy”: how does this contrast with the despair of the refrain?
What “light” and what “truth” do you need to ask God for in order to take the next step?
What did the fathers tell about the past, and how do the people describe their own trust in verses 4 to 8?
The people claim they have not betrayed the covenant and still suffer: how does this psalm question the idea that all suffering is punishment, and how does Paul use verse 22 in Romans 8?
The verb עוּר (ur, “awake”) appears in the plea “wake up, O Lord! Why do You sleep?”: how should we understand such a bold prayer within Scripture?
The psalm ends without an answer, only with a plea: do you allow yourself to pray like this when you do not understand what God is doing?
What qualities and adornments of the king are extolled in verses 2 to 9?
The king is called “God” in verse 6: how has this expression been read in the Jewish tradition, and how does the Letter to the Hebrews apply it to Jesus?
The word שֵׁבֶט (shevet, “scepter, rod”) appears twice in verse 6: what does a scepter “of justice” mean for a warrior king?
The bride is called to forget “your father's house”: what old attachments may need to be left behind to embrace a new commitment?
What natural catastrophes does the psalm imagine in verses 2 and 3, and what is the people's reaction to them?
Jerusalem had no great river: why does the psalm speak of a river that makes glad the city of God?
The verb רָפָה (rafah, “let go, relax”) lies behind “be still”: what kind of stillness does it suggest, in a psalm full of war?
In what area of your life do you need to lay down your weapons and hear “be still” in order to know that God is God?
What gestures and sounds of celebration does the psalm call for in verses 1, 5 and 6?
The nobles of the peoples gather with the people of the God of Abraham: what view of the nations appears at the end of the psalm?
The verb עָלָה (alah, “go up, ascend”) in “God has ascended amid shouts of joy”: what scene of enthronement or procession lies behind this ascent?
The psalm calls for praise “with understanding”: how do you unite emotion and understanding when you praise God?
What happens to the kings who assemble against Zion, according to verses 4 to 7?
Why does the psalm invite us to walk around Zion, count its towers and consider its ramparts, and what does this have to do with the next generation?
The word צָפוֹן (tsafon, “north”) was also the name of a sacred mountain of neighboring peoples: what effect does it have to place Zion “on the sides of the north”?
What have you been telling the next generation about what God has done?
What happens to the wise, the foolish and the rich in the face of death, according to verses 6 to 12?
Verse 15 states that God will redeem the psalmist's soul from Sheol: what hope in the face of death appears here, unlike the fate of verse 14?
The verb פָּדָה (padah, “redeem, ransom”) appears in verse 7 and verse 15: what does the psalm say money cannot redeem, and who can?
“He will take nothing with him when he dies”: how does this truth change the way you look at the wealth of others and at your own?
How does God present Himself in verses 1 to 6, and who is called as witness to the judgment?
If God does not reject the sacrifices, what does He criticize in the people's worship, and what does He ask for instead?
The word תּוֹדָה (todah, “thanksgiving, sacrifice of praise”) appears in verses 14 and 23: why is thanksgiving presented as the sacrifice God desires?
God asks the wicked why he recites His statutes: at what points are your words about God and your practice far apart?
What verbs of cleansing does David use in verses 1, 2, 7 and 9 to ask for forgiveness?
David sinned against Bathsheba and Uriah, but says “against You, You only, have I sinned”: how should we understand this statement?
The verb בָּרָא (bara, “create”) is the same as in Genesis 1:1, and in the Bible it always has God as its subject: what does it mean to ask God to create a clean heart in you?
What would it be for you to offer God “a broken and contrite heart” and not only religious gestures?
What does the psalm say about the tongue and the words of the “mighty man” in verses 1 to 4?
What contrast is there between the man who trusts in riches and the green olive tree in the house of God?
The word חֵסֵד (chesed, “loving devotion, loyal love”) appears in verse 1 and verse 8: how does it frame the psalm in contrast with boasting in evil?
The mighty man's tongue is “like a sharpened razor”: when have your words wounded someone without your noticing right away?
Compare this psalm with Psalm 14: what name of God is used here, and which verse changes most?
Verse 5 speaks of great terror “where there was nothing to fear” and of scattered bones: what historical situation or what reading does this change suggest?
The verb שָׂכַל (sakhal, “be wise, understand”) in verse 2: what kind of understanding does God look for among the sons of men?
Those who do evil “do not call on God”: what relationship do you see between ceasing to pray and ceasing to see the other?
According to the title and verse 3, who threatens David, and what does the psalmist say about their attitude toward God?
God's name appears in the plea of verse 1 and in the praise of verse 6: how does this frame sum up the movement of the psalm?
The word נְדָבָה (nedavah, “freewill offering”) in verse 6: what difference does a sacrifice offered “willingly” make?
Who in your life have been those who “sustain my soul,” and how do you give thanks for them?
Who is behind the betrayal described in verses 12 to 14, and why does it hurt more than an enemy's attack?
What desire does the psalmist express with the wings of a dove, and how does the psalm answer this longing to flee?
The word יְהָב (yehav, “burden, care”) in verse 22 speaks of what is cast on the LORD: what image of surrender does it suggest?
The psalmist prays “evening, morning and noon”: what rhythm of prayer would fit into your routine today?
What sentence about fear and trust is repeated in verses 3-4 and 10-11?
What images does verse 8 use to say that God keeps the psalmist's tears, and what do they convey about suffering?
The verb בָּטַח (batach, “trust”) appears in verses 3, 4 and 11: how does trust live alongside fear, and not merely replace it, in this psalm?
“When I am afraid, I put my trust in You”: what concrete fear could you name before God today?
What images of danger appear in verses 4 and 6, and what happens to those who dug the pit?
The refrain of verses 5 and 11 stands between danger and praise: what role does it play in the structure of the psalm?
The verb כּוּן (kun, “be steadfast”) is repeated in verse 7: how can someone hiding in a cave have a steadfast heart?
“I will awaken the dawn”: what would it be like to begin your day with praise, even before the problems pass?
Whom does the psalmist accuse in verses 1 and 2, and what images of venom and deafness does he use for them?
The pleas of verses 6 to 10 are harsh, and verse 10 speaks of washing one's feet in blood: how should we read these words, knowing that they cry out against unjust judges?
The verb שָׁפַט (shafat, “judge”) appears in verse 1, about human judges, and in verse 11, about God: what contrast does the psalm build between the two judgments?
The psalm ends with “surely there is a God who judges the earth”: how does this certainty affect the way you react to injustice?
What image is repeated in verses 6 and 14, and what does it say about the enemies?
The psalmist asks in verse 11 that the enemies not be killed and in verse 13 that they be destroyed: how should we understand this tension in the plea?
The word עֹז (oz, “strength”) appears in verses 9, 16 and 17: how does God's strength stand against the “strong” who band together against the psalmist in verse 3?
The enemies prowl at night, and the psalmist sings “in the morning”: what helps you get through the night to the morning song?
What images of defeat do the people use in verses 1 to 3?
The oracle of verses 6 to 8 lists territories of Israel and of neighboring peoples: what does it affirm about who is the true owner of the land?
The word שָׁוְא (shav, “worthless, vain”) qualifies the help of man in verse 11: how is this judgment different from despising human effort?
“With God we will perform with valor”: what challenge that seems too big could you face with this confidence?
